title: Hidden collision statistics in bosonic heat transport: Superthermal correlations at fixed mean current
authors: Iu. A. Nosal, A. E. Teretenkov
abstract: Reservoirs with the same mean relaxation rate can be indistinguishable at the level of average energy transport while producing different fluctuations. We study a bosonic mode coupled to hot and cold Poisson streams of thermal ancillas through finite beam-splitter collisions. The averaged evolution is a compound-Poisson semigroup generated by finite Gaussian event channels. Its nonequilibrium steady state is an exact mixture of thermal states governed by a random affine fixed point. Consequently, the mean-occupation dynamics and bath-resolved mean heat currents coincide with those of the matched continuous Lindblad reservoir, whereas higher correlations retain the collision strength. For equal collision transmissivities, we derive an exact superthermal bunching law controlled by the temperature contrast and collision strength. We also obtain the asymptotic rates of the first two heat cumulants for an ideal stationary event-resolved two-point-measurement record and separate local one-collision contributions from temporal correlations. Fock-space diagonalization and Monte Carlo trajectories validate the formulas and connect full resets to the weak-collision Gaussian limit.
summary: This paper analyzes bosonic heat transport through a system undergoing discrete, stochastic collisions with thermal baths. It demonstrates that while the average energy flow can be made to match a continuous model, the higher-order statistical correlations, such as heat noise, retain unique signatures dependent on the finite collision strengths. This highlights the power of fluctuation measurements to probe the microscopic details of non-equilibrium quantum processes.
main_problem: The paper investigates hidden collision statistics in bosonic heat transport, specifically examining how fluctuations (higher-order correlations) can reveal details about the underlying physical process even when the average energy transport matches a simpler continuous model.
main_result: While the mean energy and mean heat currents match between the discrete collision model and the continuous Lindblad reservoir, the higher-order correlations and heat noise retain a dependence on the finite collision strengths, proving that average measurements can mask underlying statistical differences.
method: The analysis uses theoretical derivations involving compound-Poisson semigroups, moment recursions, and comparison between discrete collision dynamics and continuous Lindblad master equations.
model_or_system: The model consists of a single bosonic mode coupled to hot and cold thermal ancillas via finite beam-splitter collisions. The dynamics are governed by a master equation representing a Poisson mixture of event channels.
key_observables: Mean-occupation dynamics, bath-resolved mean heat currents, higher-order correlations ($g^{(m)}$), and zero-frequency heat noise ($S_h$).
important_parameters: Collision transmissivity ($\eta_k$), collision strength ($q_k$), and the temperature contrast between the hot and cold baths.
main_assumptions: The comparison is made between the discrete collision process and its matched continuous Lindblad reservoir limit; the authors explicitly note that they do not derive a full fluctuation symmetry.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares the finite Poisson collision reservoir (discrete events) against the matched continuous Lindblad reference, showing that the collision model retains higher-order correlations and heat noise dependent on collision strengths.
paper_structure: The paper develops from establishing the general collision dynamics via a compound-Poisson semigroup, deriving the stationary state via random affine fixed points, and finally comparing the resulting mean observables and higher-order cumulants against the continuous limit.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant for AMO and open quantum systems as it provides a rigorous framework for distinguishing between different physical mechanisms (discrete vs. continuous) in energy transport using fluctuation measurements, which is a key area in quantum thermodynamics.
